sections.heading: What progress looks like, in criterion terms, after a month
paragraphs: Four weeks in, look at a task rather than a grade. Your child should annotate the task sheet before starting, and you should be able to see the annotations. The command term should be identified and the required skill named. In a mathematics investigation there should be an attempt at a general rule rather than three worked examples. In a science task there should be a sentence about why a variable was controlled. These are visible on the page to a parent who has never taught anything.

By the end of a term the criterion levels should move unevenly, and that is normal rather than disappointing. The criterion that was worked on improves first and the others follow, because the underlying skill is reading what is being asked. Ask the subject teacher at the next meeting whether the student is now addressing the criterion, which is a question they can answer precisely, rather than asking whether the child has improved, which invites a polite generality.

Over a full Middle Years Programme year, the honest account of what tutoring did is specific. The student learned to read a task and plan against it. One or two criteria that were consistently weak became reliable. Content gaps that were blocking progress were closed. Written reflection stopped being an afterthought. What tutoring did not do is change the child's ability, replace the school's teaching, or support a prediction. IB Gram does not guarantee grades, and in a criterion-based programme a promised grade is especially meaningless.

The limit worth naming is about volume. A Middle Years Programme student has eight subject groups and no family can tutor all of them, nor should they try. Two subjects at a time, chosen for the widest criterion gap, with the skills deliberately transferred to the others by the student themselves, is the arrangement that works. Families across Mumbai who hire four home tutors for a thirteen-year-old usually end the year with a tired child and the same report.

sections.heading: Starting MYP home tuition in Cumballa Hill
paragraphs: Bring three documents. The last report with the criterion levels, not just the subject grades. The most recent marked task with its task-specific clarification sheet, which is the document that makes everything else interpretable. And the school's assessment calendar for the term, so the tutor can work ahead of the next task rather than behind the last one. Most families have the first and have thrown away the second, which is worth knowing before the session.

Expect the first session to be mostly watching. The tutor will ask your child to attempt part of a task, or to redo a paragraph, and will read how the instruction was interpreted rather than whether the content was right. That is where the criterion gap becomes visible. A tutor who spends ninety minutes explaining a topic to a Middle Years Programme student has not yet found out what the problem is.

By the end you should hear whether this is a content problem or a criterion problem, which criteria are being targeted first, what work will be set between sessions and when it will be read. Ask also for the short version in your child's words: a twelve-year-old who can say what criterion B asks for has already gained something. A home tutor for MYP subject groups in Mumbai who cannot produce that in one session is unlikely to produce it in ten.

Then keep it small and regular. Two short slots a week if the tutor is local enough, the rubric on the table every time, a midweek check on a plan rather than a finished piece, and a review at four weeks against the markers above. The Middle Years Programme rewards habits more than hours, and habits are built in short weekly repetitions. Home classes in Cumballa Hill work when a household can sustain them for five years without thinking about it, which is a lower bar than most Mumbai parents set themselves.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our building straight after school?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and for this age group it is the slot worth fighting for. School runs around the hill are short, so many children are home by late afternoon, and a tutor based in Kemps Corner, Breach Candy, Tardeo or near Grant Road can take a five o'clock start. A Middle Years Programme student at five is a different person from the same student at eight, when homework is finished and attention has gone. Ask for the early slot when the match is made, because across Mumbai it is the first one to fill.

faqs.question: Should a parent sit in on a session at home for a younger child?
faqs.answer: For the first session, briefly, then no. An adult in the house is sensible for an eleven or twelve-year-old, but sitting in changes how a child answers questions and makes most of them perform rather than think. The better arrangement is to be available for two minutes at the end so the tutor can tell you what happened and what has been set. For online sessions the rule is firmer: somebody in the house, the work on a table, and the camera on the page.

faqs.question: My child got a middling grade in a subject she works hard at. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: Usually that one criterion is pulling the grade down rather than that the subject is not understood. Because a Middle Years Programme grade is built by converting criterion levels, a student strong in knowing and understanding and weak in investigating or evaluating can look average overall while being genuinely good at the content. Ask the teacher which criteria were assessed this term and which level was awarded in each. That answer tells you what to work on; the subject grade on its own tells you almost nothing.

faqs.question: What is a task-specific clarification and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: It is the version of the criterion wording adapted to the particular task your child has been set, and it describes what reaching each band looks like for that piece of work. It matters because students who do not read it answer a slightly different question from the one being marked, and lose levels they could have had. Keep every one of these sheets. Handing a tutor the marked task plus its clarification is worth more than a whole conversation about how the term has gone.

faqs.question: Is tutoring necessary in the MYP if there are no external exams?
faqs.answer: Necessary is too strong, but the Middle Years Programme years are where help is cheapest and most durable. The criterion skills, reasoning in writing, generalising, evaluating, weighing evidence, are precisely what the Diploma Programme and the Cambridge courses both assess more heavily later, so fixing them at thirteen costs a fraction of fixing them at seventeen. The absence of an external examination makes nothing feel urgent, which is why families wait, and why waiting is expensive.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an MYP student need?
faqs.answer: Two short ones in a subject being actively repaired, or one in a subject being maintained. Fifty-minute sessions suit this age group far better than ninety-minute ones, and frequency does more than duration because the skill being taught is a habit. Two subjects at a time is the practical ceiling for most thirteen-year-olds who also have sport, music and eight subject groups of homework. Adding a third tutor usually reduces the return on the first two.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the personal project?
faqs.answer: At the start and at the end, and never in the middle of the making. The useful help is pressure-testing the goal so it is specific and achievable, keeping the process journal honest while the work happens, and reading the final report against the criteria to say where the reflection is thin. The decisions, the product and the writing must be the student's own, and the school supervises the academic honesty requirements. A tutor who offers to help build or write it is creating a problem, not solving one.

faqs.question: Does the MYP prepare a student for the Diploma Programme?
faqs.answer: For the thinking, yes; for the examination conditions, less so. Middle Years Programme students arrive in the Diploma Programme with genuinely good inquiry and writing habits and often with very little experience of a timed paper or of revising a large body of content. That gap is the commonest cause of a poor first Diploma Programme term in students who were strong at fifteen. Year 5 is the time to add timed practice, and it is even more important for a student moving onto a Cambridge route instead.

faqs.question: Should we start examination technique in Year 5?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the second half of it, and the reason depends on where your child is going next. A student continuing into the Diploma Programme needs practice at writing under time and at revising cumulatively, neither of which the programme emphasises. A student moving onto a Cambridge route needs more: recall under pressure, mark-scheme discipline and whole-paper stamina. Either way the work is light, perhaps a session a fortnight across the final months, and it prevents a bad first term that takes a year to recover.

faqs.question: What do IB tuition fees in Cumballa Hill depend on for MYP?
faqs.answer: Year group and subject group first, since language acquisition and specialist arts experience is scarcer than general science or mathematics teaching. Then local availability, travel time at peak hour, session length and frequency, and how much reading happens between sessions. For this programme the frequency question matters most: two short sessions a week will cost more in total than one long one, and for an eleven or thirteen-year-old it is usually the better purchase. Compare quotes on the same weekly structure.

faqs.question: Can you tell us whether my child will reach the top band?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not guarantee grades, and in a criterion-based programme a predicted level is even less meaningful than elsewhere, because the levels awarded depend on which criteria each task assesses. What a tutor can tell you after one session is which criterion is costing the most, what the first four weeks will target, and what you should see on the page by then. For a realistic view of where your child sits, the subject teacher holds the full record of criterion levels across the year.

sections.heading: What does MYP ask of a Year 1 to Year 5 student?
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme covers Years 1 to 5 and sits between the Primary Years Programme (PYP) and the Diploma Programme (DP), with Year 5 as the exit into DP1. It is not built like an examination syllabus. Its explicit purpose is to develop approaches to learning: research, communication, self-management, thinking and social skills, taught inside subjects rather than beside them. The assessment reflects that, marking against task-specific descriptors instead of a content checklist.

What it asks of a student, concretely, is attention over time. Finding sources and judging them. Planning before writing. Drafting, then revising rather than extending. Evaluating a conclusion instead of restating a question. Keeping a record of a process while the process is happening. None of these are quick-fire skills and none of them survive a noisy half hour. This is the part of the programme that most often fails quietly in a Mumbai flat, and it is mistaken for a lack of ability far more often than it should be.

Which is why the environment here matters beyond comfort. In a genuinely quiet room, an MYP tutor can set a twenty-five minute block of silent reading or drafting and then work on what the student produced, which is the closest thing the programme has to a core exercise. In a busy flat the same tutor spends that time managing interruptions and ends up talking instead, and talking is the one mode that teaches none of the five skills. It is the clearest practical reason to engage an IB MYP home tutor in Dadar Parsi Colony rather than a general tuition class near the station. For the current structure of MYP assessment and whether your school uses eAssessment at the end of Year 5, ask your MYP coordinator rather than relying on anything written online.

sections.heading: Eight subject groups, four criteria, one session a week
paragraphs: MYP organises learning into eight subject groups: Language and Literature, Language Acquisition, Individuals and Societies, Sciences, Mathematics, Arts, Physical and Health Education, and Design. Each is assessed against four criteria labelled A to D, and the descriptors differ by group. Sciences covers knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Mathematics covers knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts.

With one session a week, a tutor has to choose. The useful choice is almost always the criterion where the gap is widest rather than the subject where the mark is lowest, and those are frequently different things. A Year 4 student who can execute mathematical procedures but writes solutions nobody could follow is weak in communicating, not in Mathematics, and the same weakness will be costing her marks in Sciences and in Individuals and Societies. One criterion, three subject groups. Fixing it once is a term's work; fixing it three times is not.

So ask any MYP subject groups tutor in Dadar Parsi Colony to look at the last two returned tasks from different subjects and say whether the same criterion appears in both. That is the single most useful twenty minutes a tutor can spend before planning anything. Interdisciplinary units are the other place to look, because they assess two subject groups together and reward connecting them rather than covering each. Students who are competent in both separately sometimes come apart there, and it is nearly always a planning problem rather than a knowledge one.

The shape of the year in Mumbai, Maharashtra goes roughly like this. The opening term is quiet in assessment terms and is the cheapest time to build habits, which is exactly when almost nobody calls. Summative tasks then cluster at the close of each unit, so the pressure arrives in waves specific to your child's timetable rather than on predictable dates. A Year 2 or Year 3 student is still learning to sit down, begin and keep going, and self-management is explicitly one of the skills being developed. Hybrid suits Year 5 and the personal project particularly well. The planning and reflection conversations want eye contact and a quiet room, both of which this colony supplies. sections.heading: Has this tutor ever marked a criterion grid?
paragraphs: That is the question that matters most here and it is not answered by a qualification. We check identity against a government photo document, qualifications against the certificates themselves, and teaching claims against the specific programme and years claimed. In MYP that last check does more work than anywhere else, because a great many competent tutors have taught IGCSE or Diploma Programme content for years and have never marked against MYP criteria. Content knowledge and criterion fluency are different things, and only one of them shows on a curriculum vitae.

Run two checks yourself on the discovery call. Ask the tutor to name the four criteria for the subject group in question and say what each one actually rewards; someone with real MYP experience answers without pausing. Then show them a returned task and ask which criterion cost the most and why. An IB private tutor Dadar Parsi Colony families found through a neighbour may be a fine teacher of content and still fail both questions, which is much better to learn in twenty minutes than in two terms.

What no process can verify is whether your fourteen-year-old will tell this adult that they do not understand something. In the middle years that is close to decisive, and it is why we would rather your child joined the call. We also contact family references and ask about punctuality and consistency rather than only about results. Be wary of any tutor who offers a guaranteed grade, quotes a success rate or implies a relationship with a named school. A home tutor for MYP subject groups Mumbai parents should trust talks in detail about criteria and declines to predict outcomes.

sections.heading: The personal project is a project management problem
paragraphs: In Year 5 the personal project asks a student to plan, carry out and reflect on a substantial piece of independent work largely under their own management. Almost every difficulty families report with it is managerial rather than intellectual. The question is too broad to answer. The success criteria were never defined, so nothing can be judged complete. The process record was reconstructed at the end instead of kept as the work happened. The reflection repeats the plan rather than examining what diverged from it.

A tutor's job here is to be the person who asks awkward questions early. What will exist at the end that does not exist now? How will you know it is good? What is the first thing you will do, this week, and how long will it take? Which part are you least confident about, and what happens if it fails? Those four questions, asked in the first fortnight, prevent most of the Year 5 distress that arrives in the last month. They are also the questions nobody enjoys answering, which is why an adult outside the family often gets further with them than a parent does.

This is where the colony's quiet pays off most visibly. Project work needs long uninterrupted blocks, and a student with a closable room and large flat can do forty-five minutes of genuine drafting while a tutor sits and works alongside them, then spend the rest of the session reviewing what came out. That working-alongside mode is impossible in a busy room and it is the single most effective use of an hour with an IB MYP home tutor in Dadar Parsi Colony in Year 5. The tutor contributes nothing to the content, which is the rule: challenge and supervision only, never writing, editing or supplying material, because the project is assessed as the student's own work.

sections.heading: What should change by the fourth week?
paragraphs: The work, not the level. Four weeks in, a returned task should show reasoning written down where there was previously only an answer, a source referred to and questioned rather than simply quoted, and a conclusion that says something the question did not already say. The strongest single test is to ask your child which criterion the teacher was unhappy with on the last task. A child who can answer that has understood how they are being marked, and in the Middle Years Programme that understanding is most of the battle.

By one term, levels in the targeted subject group should be moving, though unevenly, because criteria are assessed on different tasks at different points. Across a full year the realistic outcome is a student who reads a task sheet and can say what each criterion wants before starting, plus a personal project begun early enough to be finished without panic. That is the honest extent of it. IB Gram does not guarantee grades or levels, and no tutor working through this platform may suggest otherwise to you or to your child.

When it is not working, say so in week three rather than month three. In MYP the usual cause is register: a tutor pitching at examination standard to a child who needs a task unpicked slowly, or treating a Year 5 student like a Year 2 one. Tell us what happens in the room and we will either ask for a change of approach or return to the shortlist for a replacement, with no notice period. The second most common cause, worth naming because parents feel awkward raising it, is the slot: even here, a session placed after a long day and a sports practice is an hour of poor attention.

faqs.answer: One that can be closed, which this colony supplies more often than most of Mumbai does. The low-rise layout and large old flats mean a child usually has a room, or a defined corner of one, where traffic noise does not reach. That matters because MYP work needs uninterrupted blocks: twenty-five minutes of silent drafting or reading, then review. Settle the room in session one and keep it the same each week.

faqs.question: My child's MYP levels look average. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It can be, and mid-range levels are the hardest signal in the programme to read. A student can clear the lower descriptors comfortably for years while never writing a genuine evaluation or questioning a source, and that reads as unremarkable rather than as a warning. The thing to read instead is the teacher comments. If the same remark about unsupported conclusions or insufficient evaluation appears across two subject groups and two years, it describes a habit. Habits take a term to change in Year 3 and considerably longer once DP1 has started.

faqs.question: What are criteria A to D and why do they matter?
faqs.answer: They are the four assessment criteria each MYP subject group is marked against, and the descriptors differ by group. Sciences covers knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Mathematics covers knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. They matter because one weak criterion can drag an otherwise capable student, and because the same weak criterion usually shows up across several subjects. Your MYP coordinator can give you the current descriptors for each group your child takes.

faqs.question: How much can a tutor help with the personal project?
faqs.answer: Supervision and challenge, and nothing else. The project is assessed as the student's own planning, execution and reflection, so a tutor who contributes content or writing creates an academic honesty problem rather than solving an academic one. What a good tutor does is refuse an overly broad question, insist the success criteria are defined before work starts, make sure the process record is kept as the work happens, and ask what happens if the hardest part fails. Ask any shortlisted tutor where they draw that line before lessons begin.

faqs.question: Will MYP tutoring prepare my child for DP1?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the useful part is rarely more content. The gap students hit in DP1 is precision and stamina: producing correct concise answers under time pressure, and sustaining a long independent piece for Theory of Knowledge (TOK) and the Extended Essay (EE). So in the second half of Year 5 the valuable work is timed practice on material already known, notes a stranger could read, and one piece of writing longer than feels necessary. A tutor who spends that term covering ahead into Diploma content is usually solving the wrong problem.

faqs.answer: Less well than a tutor in the room, and it is fair to say so plainly. Younger MYP students need someone present to notice the blank page and the drifting attention, and that noticing is a large part of the self-management the programme is trying to build. From Year 4 onwards online becomes genuinely viable and is sometimes the only route to a specialist in a thinner subject group such as Design or Arts. faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking rather than assuming. faqs.question: Is it worth starting in Year 1 or Year 2?
faqs.answer: It can be, though for a different reason than parents expect. At that stage the work is almost never subject content; it is learning to start a task, keep a record, and read a task sheet properly. A short weekly session that builds those three things is cheap insurance against a Year 5 personal project going badly. paragraphs: The input that makes this match work is the report card itself, with the criterion levels on it, rather than a sentence saying your child is struggling in science. Two students with the same subject grade can have opposite profiles. An IB MYP tutor in Dadar matched on the grade alone is being matched on a number that has already discarded the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Years 1 to 5: how does the Middle Years Programme actually work?
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme runs across five years and eight subject groups: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Each subject group is assessed against four criteria, usually labelled A to D, each with its own published descriptors describing what work at each level looks like. Teaching is organised around units with a statement of inquiry and a global context rather than around chapters, which is why a Middle Years exercise book looks nothing like the one you remember.

The single most important thing to understand is that a criterion level is a band, not a fraction. A level of five out of eight is not sixty-two per cent and is not a near miss. Each level has a written descriptor, and moving up a band means doing something qualitatively different rather than doing the same thing more accurately. Parents who read the numbers as percentages reliably conclude their child is mid-table in everything, which is almost never what the profile actually says.

Years 1 to 3 are where habits are built and where the programme is most forgiving. Years 4 and 5 are where the demands sharpen: longer written tasks, more independent investigation, and in Year 5 the personal project. Some schools also enter students for on-screen assessments and portfolio assessment leading to a formal Middle Years certificate, and some do not. Ask your school which route it follows, because it changes what the final year looks like considerably. Do not take deadlines, weightings or structures from this page; the IB revises programme documentation on its own cycle, so confirm with your school's MYP coordinator.

This page is about the Middle Years Programme only. The Diploma years and the Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel route belong to sibling pages, and MYP home tuition in Dadar aimed at a Year 3 student should not be a Diploma course delivered early. The preparation that actually helps is in the next sections, and it is about thinking skills rather than about content your child will meet anyway.

sections.heading: The eight MYP subject groups and the criterion each one neglects
paragraphs: Across the report cards we read, one pattern repeats in almost every subject group: criterion A is taught thoroughly and the later criteria are assessed without ever having been taught. In mathematics the criteria cover knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. School lessons concentrate on the first. A student who can solve every equation set for her will still score poorly on investigating patterns, because nobody has shown her how to form a general rule from a sequence of cases and then justify it. That is a teachable skill and it is where an MYP subject groups tutor in Dadar does the most visible work.

In the sciences the criteria cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The second and third are laboratory-skills criteria and they reward specific moves: naming a controlled variable rather than listing equipment, explaining why a method is reliable rather than asserting that it is, evaluating a result against a hypothesis rather than describing what happened. Students lose levels here while knowing the science perfectly.

In language and literature the criteria cover analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. The reliable loss is analysing: students summarise a text and believe they have analysed it. Analysis requires naming a choice the writer made and saying what effect it has, and the difference between those two activities is the entire gap between a middling level and a strong one. Individuals and societies follows the same pattern, where thinking critically is the neglected criterion and the fix is being taught to weigh two sources against each other rather than to report both.

The practical consequence is that a parent should not ask for a tutor in a subject. Ask for a tutor for a criterion. A home tutor for MYP subject groups in Mumbai who begins by teaching more content to a student whose criterion A is already strong will produce a happier child and an unchanged report. MYP subject groups home classes Dadar parents book should start from the lowest criterion level on the card and work on that specifically for the first month.

sections.heading: What does a Mumbai MYP report card actually tell you?
paragraphs: More than parents think and less than they fear. Children in this part of the city attend a small set of international schools, with Don Bosco International School in Matunga and JBCN International School, Parel coming up most often on our calls from Dadar. IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with Don Bosco International School, JBCN International School, Parel, or any school named here. We name them because their reporting cycles and their criterion comments are what families here are trying to interpret.

Read the card by criterion rather than by subject. Four levels across a subject group describe a shape, and the shape is the information. Strong A with weak D says the content is secure and the thinking has not been asked for. Weak A with strong C says your child writes well about material she has not learned. Even levels across all four usually mean the teacher is averaging rather than assessing, and that is worth a polite question at the parent meeting rather than a tutor.

Read the comments literally. Criterion comments are written against descriptors, so a phrase like needs to justify conclusions is not a generality. It names the specific move that separates two bands, and a tutor who knows the descriptors can convert that phrase into four weeks of concrete work. This is the main reason we insist on seeing the card rather than a summary of it.

The reporting calendar also decides timing. Most Mumbai international schools report two or three times a year, and the useful moment to hire is immediately after a report rather than immediately before the next one, because you then have a full cycle to change the thing the card named. Starting home tutoring in Mumbai three weeks before a reporting deadline produces a tutor doing triage on a piece of coursework instead of work that changes a level.

sections.heading: Should MYP home classes in Dadar be at home or online?
paragraphs: At home for Years 1 to 3 almost without exception, and mostly at home for Years 4 and 5. The reason is attention rather than content. A twelve year old working with a tutor on a screen is a twelve year old with a device in front of her and a tab she can reach, and the supervision that makes a session productive at that age is physical presence. A tutor at your table also sees the things that explain a report card: the book bag that has no system in it, the homework diary nobody fills in, the unit folder with loose sheets.

There is a second reason specific to this programme. Middle Years work is produced rather than answered. A student assembles a design folder, a science investigation, an analysis of a text, and the tutor's job is often to look at a half-finished artefact spread across a table and ask what is missing. Paper spread out beats a shared screen for that, and it is why IB home tuition in Dadar remains the right default for this age group even when the family is comfortable with online lessons.

Online earns a narrow place. For a Year 5 student working on a long piece, a short screen slot to discuss a draft the tutor has already read offline is efficient and avoids an unnecessary journey. For a scarce language or an arts subject where no local specialist exists, online is the only option and is better than nothing. And in the monsoon, an online session keeps a week intact rather than losing it. An IB online tutor in Dadar is a reasonable supplement at this stage and a poor primary mode.

The honest cost. An IB private tutor Dadar families engage for an early evening slot is being paid for a journey made at an awkward hour, and in Mumbai, Maharashtra that hour is the most expensive part of the arrangement whether or not the quote says so. Online removes it and removes the supervision that a younger student actually needs. For Years 1 to 3 the sensible answer is to pay for presence.

sections.heading: What to check before an MYP tutor comes to your Mumbai flat
paragraphs: We verify identity against government photo identification, qualification against the original degree certificate rather than a claim on a form, and programme experience in a conversation specific enough to separate a teacher who has assessed Middle Years work against criteria from one who has taught the same content in another system. An IB MYP tutor in Dadar who cannot explain what distinguishes two adjacent levels in a criterion she has taught does not reach your shortlist.

With a younger child there is a second layer and you should apply it yourself. Does the tutor speak to your daughter or about her? Does she ask the child what she thinks the comment on her work means, or explain it over her head to you? Can she run a forty-minute session with a tired twelve year old without either losing the room or entertaining her? Those are the things that decide whether this works, and no certificate speaks to any of them.

Four questions for the call. Which subject groups and which Middle Years years have you taught? What does criterion B ask for in your subject, in plain words? What would you do in the first month with a student whose criterion A is strong and criterion D is weak? And how will you report to me? The second question is the sharpest filter available, because a tutor who answers it in the language of the descriptors has done this and one who answers with a topic list has not.

Two red flags. A tutor who talks about results in aggregate rather than about your child's criterion profile, and anyone who indicates a future grade before seeing any work. No honest tutor offers a guaranteed grade, and we do not guarantee grades either. The best IB tutor in Dadar for a Middle Years child is often not the most academically impressive candidate on the list but the one who can hold the attention of a thirteen year old at six in the evening and still demand something of her.

sections.heading: The personal project in Year 5, and the jump into the Diploma
paragraphs: The personal project is the piece of Middle Years work that worries families most and prepares students best. In the final year each student chooses a goal, keeps a process journal while working towards it, produces an outcome, and writes a report assessed against criteria. The subject is the student's own choice, which is exactly why it goes wrong: a goal chosen because it sounds impressive produces a journal with nothing in it, and the report is marked on the process rather than on the product. A spectacular outcome with a thin journal scores badly. A modest outcome with an honest, detailed journal scores well.

A tutor's role here is narrow and genuinely useful. She can challenge a goal that is too large to document, insist the journal is kept weekly rather than reconstructed in the last fortnight, ask what evidence exists for each claim the report will make, and point out when a student is describing what she made rather than reflecting on how she made it. She cannot choose the goal, produce the outcome or write the report, and your school's academic honesty policy and supervisor arrangements govern all of this. Confirm the boundaries with the MYP coordinator rather than with a tutor.

The second worry is the transition into the Diploma Programme, and the honest version is that the jump is about volume and self-management rather than conceptual difficulty. A Middle Years student is used to work that is produced over weeks with feedback along the way. A Diploma student faces external examinations, more content per subject, and internally assessed work with a fixed deadline and much less scaffolding. Students who struggle in the first Diploma term are usually not short of ability; they are short of a note-taking system, a way of meeting a deadline without a reminder, and the habit of reading a mark scheme.

The preparation that works is therefore not early Diploma content. It is six or eight sessions aimed at the subjects your child will take at Higher Level, spent on independent working habits: notes that remain usable three months later, a weekly plan she writes herself, and one piece of long-form writing taken from draft to final without being chased. MYP home tuition in Dadar aimed at those three things changes a first Diploma term far more than a head start on the syllabus would.

A weekly journal beats a reconstructed one in the final fortnight

sections.heading: What MYP home tuition changes across one reporting cycle in Mumbai
paragraphs: At four weeks you are checking fit, and the signals for a younger student are different from those for a Diploma one. Your child should be able to say what she is working on and why, in her own words rather than as a subject name. Work should be going into a folder with some system to it. The tutor should have named one criterion as the target and should be able to show you a piece of work that moved on it. And your child should mildly dislike at least part of the session, because a Middle Years session that is entirely pleasant is usually not demanding anything.

Across one reporting cycle, which in most Mumbai schools means a term or a semester, the realistic target is one criterion moving a band in one subject group. That sounds modest and it is the right ambition. Criterion movement is qualitative: it means the student has started doing something she was not doing before, such as justifying a conclusion or naming a controlled variable, and once she does it in one subject she usually starts doing it in others without being told. That spillover is the real return.

Across the full programme the honest answer is a range and the gains compound in habits rather than in grades. IB tuition fees in Dadar buy contact hours and an outside adult who reads the criterion descriptors. They do not buy a level. We do not publish success rates and we do not guarantee grades, because an average across unlike students is a marketing number rather than information about your child, and because a Middle Years level depends on work produced over months in school rather than on anything that happens at your dining table.

The warning sign is a tutor who talks about the subject and never about the criteria. If at week six the conversation is still about covering more science, the report card will say the same thing next cycle. Ask which criterion is the target, what the descriptor for the next band requires, and what evidence exists that your child is closer to it. Parents searching for IB tutors near me in Dadar often fear a change means starting over; from an existing shortlist it is normally about a week.

faqs.question: My son's report shows levels of 6, 5, 5 and 3. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It means his content knowledge is solid and one specific kind of thinking has not been taught or asked for. The four numbers are criterion levels, each with its own written descriptor, and they are bands rather than percentages, so a 3 is not thirty per cent. The shape is the information: a high first criterion with a low fourth usually means your son can learn material and has not been shown how to apply it to an unfamiliar situation or weigh two positions against each other. That is teachable and it is where a tutor should start.

faqs.question: Can a tutor travel to Matunga for an early evening slot before homework?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is the slot worth fighting for with a Middle Years child, because attention after eight in the evening is poor. Matunga is walkable from the station and from Dadar Parsi Colony, and because both suburban lines stop at this interchange tutors arrive without changing trains, which is what makes a five or half past five start realistic. Ask whether the tutor has a later booking nearby that same evening, because an early slot that makes her evening work is one she will protect.

faqs.question: Is a criterion level the same as a percentage?
faqs.answer: No, and reading it as one is the single most common misunderstanding among Middle Years parents. Each criterion is marked against published descriptors, and each level describes a qualitatively different kind of work rather than a quantity of correct answers. Moving up a band means doing something new, such as justifying a conclusion instead of stating it, not doing the same thing more accurately. The school converts the criterion levels into a subject grade using published boundaries. Ask your child's teacher what the next band's descriptor requires, in plain words, and you will have the whole plan.

faqs.question: How much help is allowed with the personal project?
faqs.answer: Supervision and challenge, not production. A tutor can question whether a goal is documentable, insist the process journal is kept weekly, ask what evidence supports each claim the report will make, and point out when a student is describing rather than reflecting. A tutor cannot choose the goal, make the outcome or write the report. Your school appoints a supervisor and has its own academic honesty policy and declaration process, and that policy governs. Confirm the boundaries with the Middle Years coordinator rather than relying on a tutor's interpretation.

faqs.question: Should we start tutoring before the Diploma Programme begins?
faqs.answer: Yes, and aim it at working habits rather than at content. The jump into the Diploma is about volume and self-management: more material per subject, external examinations, and internally assessed work with real deadlines and much less scaffolding than Middle Years tasks carry. Six or eight sessions over a summer, focused on the subjects your child will take at Higher Level, should produce a note-taking system that still works in three months, a weekly plan she writes herself, and one long piece taken from draft to final without being chased.

faqs.question: What do MYP tuition fees depend on in this area?
faqs.answer: Five things. The subject group, since specialists in arts, design and less common languages are scarcer than in mathematics or science. The year, where the final Middle Years year commands more because of the personal project. The hour, because early evening slots are genuinely harder to staff than later ones. Session length and weekly frequency. And travel, which this interchange compresses. Ask whether reading and commenting on work between sessions is included, since in this programme the work is produced over weeks and that reading is where much of the value sits.

faqs.question: Do I need to be at home during a Middle Years session?
faqs.answer: Yes, more than at Diploma level. For Years 1 to 3 stay in the flat and within earshot, not in the room. A younger student works better knowing a parent is present and worse with one watching. The handover at the end matters more at this age too: ask which criterion was worked on and what specifically changed, and ask your child separately what she thinks she did differently. If the two answers do not match, that is worth a conversation with the tutor rather than with the child.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring work for a Year 2 Middle Years student?
faqs.answer: Poorly, and we would rather say so. A younger student online is a student with a device in front of her and other tabs within reach, and the supervision that makes a session productive at that age is physical. Middle Years work is also produced rather than answered, so a tutor often needs to look at a half-finished folder spread across a table and ask what is missing. Keep sessions at home for the early years and use online only to keep a monsoon week intact or to reach a scarce subject specialist.

faqs.question: My daughter in Prabhadevi says she does not know what the teacher wants. What is that?
faqs.answer: Usually a criterion she has never had explained to her in plain language. Middle Years tasks are assessed against descriptors, and a student who has not read them is guessing at what counts. The fix is concrete: get the descriptor for the criterion she scores lowest on, read it with her, and convert each phrase into something she can actually do. Most students find this clarifying rather than tedious, and it often produces more improvement in a fortnight than a term of additional content teaching would.

faqs.question: What if there is no change after one reporting cycle?
faqs.answer: Ask which criterion was the target, what the next band's descriptor requires, and what evidence exists that your child is closer to it. If the answers are about covering more content, the tutor has been teaching a subject rather than a criterion and you should re-match. If the answers are specific but the level has not moved, remember that a level depends on work produced in school over months, so a habit established at your table shows up a cycle later. Tell us either way and re-matching takes about a week.

paragraphs: We match on the criterion, not the subject. An IB MYP home tutor in Dahisar who is excellent at building subject knowledge is the right choice for a student weak in criterion A and the wrong choice for one losing marks in the criterion about communicating or about reflecting. Those are different skills taught by different people. So the first thing we ask for is a photograph of the report or the marked task, letters and all, rather than a summary of how the term went.

The sequence runs like this. 1. Send the MYP year, the subject group, and the criterion letters from the most recent marked task. 2. Parents frequently arrive convinced the problem is the subject when the pattern across subjects says otherwise. A student scoring well in the knowing-and-understanding criterion across three subject groups and poorly in the communicating criterion across the same three does not have a science problem or a mathematics problem. sections.heading: The eight MYP subject groups, and which ones families here actually ask about
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme (MYP) runs for five years between the Primary Years Programme (PYP) and the Diploma Programme (DP), and organises learning into eight subject groups: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Students take work from all eight, which is the single structural fact most parents moving in from another system find hardest to accept, because it means there is no early narrowing to the subjects a child is good at.

In practice the requests we receive in this part of Mumbai cluster in four of the eight. Mathematics, because the investigating-patterns work is unlike anything in a conventional syllabus. Sciences, because the design-an-investigation criterion asks eleven-year-olds to do something most adults cannot. Language and literature, because analysis of a text is a skill rather than content and cannot be revised. And language acquisition, usually when a family has moved between cities or countries and a child has been placed in a phase that does not match her actual level.

In the final MYP year the personal project sits alongside the subject groups and casts a long shadow over the year. A student chooses a goal, keeps a process journal while working towards it, produces something, and reports on the whole thing against criteria. It is assessed on the process at least as much as on the product, which is why the most common failure is a beautiful outcome with a journal written in the last fortnight. A tutor's useful role here is scheduling and questioning, never making.

Some schools enter students for on-screen MYP assessment at the end of the programme and some award course results internally, and the arrangement differs between schools a few minutes apart in Mumbai. Criterion names, the number of criteria in a subject group and the structure of final assessment are set by the IB and revised on its own cycle, so ask your MYP coordinator for the current subject-group guide and the school's own assessment arrangements rather than relying on what an older sibling experienced.

sections.heading: Criteria A to D: how to read an MYP report that has no percentages
paragraphs: An MYP report is more useful than a percentage and almost nobody uses it. Each subject group marks against four criteria, each criterion has its own name within that subject, and each is reported as a band rather than a mark out of a hundred. A student with a strong knowing-and-understanding band and a weak communicating band is not an average student. She knows the content and cannot present it, which is a completely different problem from a student with the opposite profile, and the two need opposite first months.

The criterion names differ by subject group and that is the part parents find confusing. In sciences the four cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In mathematics they cover knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In language and literature they cover analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. The names change; the principle does not. Each criterion is a separate skill and a band in one tells you nothing about the others.

The document that matters most is the one families never see: the task-specific clarification. For each assessed task, the teacher rewrites the generic criterion descriptors to describe what the top band looks like for that particular task. It is handed out with the assignment and it is, in effect, the markscheme. An MYP subject groups tutor in Dahisar who asks for it before planning anything is doing the single highest-value thing available. A tutor who works from a textbook instead is guessing at what is being marked.

Command terms carry real weight at this level too, and they are not the same as the DP set. Identify, describe, explain, analyse, evaluate, justify, synthesise: each asks for a different quantity of reasoning, and a student who writes a description where analysis was asked for has capped her band before she started. Twenty minutes a week spent matching command terms to the kind of answer they require moves bands across every subject group at once, which is why we treat it as general work rather than subject work.

sections.heading: What does the MYP year look like at a school in Dahisar East?
paragraphs: It looks like a steady stream of assessed tasks rather than two examination seasons, and that is the most important thing for a parent to understand. MYP assessment is continuous: units end with tasks marked against criteria, reports collate those bands, and there is no single term where everything is decided. The pressure points are therefore spread through the year and cluster whenever two or three subject groups end units in the same fortnight. Your school publishes its own assessment calendar, and it is the only authority on when those fortnights fall.

Dahisar carries real MYP demand for a specific reason. JBCN International School, Borivali adds further IB cohorts minutes down the highway. For tutoring this matters directly: MYP teaching is a specialism, and tutors keep it only where they use it weekly. In most suburbs this far from the city's international-school belt, a parent asking for MYP help is offered a conventional subject tutor instead.

IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with Singapore International School, with JBCN International School, Borivali, or with any other school named on this page. We name them because their calendars and their coordinators set the terms of the work. The practical consequence of continuous assessment is that the best time to act is a single bad criterion band, not a bad report. A band is a diagnosis of one skill on one task, and fixing it takes a few weeks. By the time a report shows a pattern across three subject groups, the same skill has been missing for two terms and the student has learned a way of working around it. Families who bring us a single marked task get more out of an IB tutor Mumbai parents would recommend than families who wait for the summary.

sections.heading: Does MYP home tuition work better than online for a Year 3 student?
paragraphs: For almost every MYP student below the final year, yes, and the reason is attention rather than technology. A thirteen-year-old working on an investigation plan at a shared table drifts within ten minutes of being left alone with a screen, and the tutor cannot see it happening. Home classes put an adult in the room whose only job for that hour is noticing when she has stopped thinking. That is most of what you are paying for in the middle years, and it does not transmit over video.

There is a second, more practical argument. MYP work is physical: a process journal, a design folder, an annotated text, a plan with crossings-out. A tutor at the table can pick up the journal and see that three weeks are missing. On a video call he sees whatever is held up to the camera, which is the tidy page. Families booking IB home tuition in Dahisar for MYP work are often surprised how much of the first session is just the tutor looking through folders the student would not have volunteered.

Online earns its place in the senior MYP years and in two specific situations before then. If a child is in a language acquisition phase that nobody local teaches, an IB online tutor in Dahisar may be the only route to the right specialist. And for personal project supervision in the final year, short frequent online check-ins work well, because the useful intervention is a fifteen-minute question about the journal rather than an hour of teaching. Both work provided the tutor sees the actual documents in advance.

Online is the wrong choice for a Year 1 or Year 2 MYP student who cannot yet work alone, and we will say so rather than take the easier booking. The arrangement that holds here is in-person weekly for the main subject group plus occasional online check-ins near a task deadline. Parents comparing a nearby group class should ask whether the class has read the task-specific clarification for their child's assignment. A group of fifteen students on three different tasks cannot have.

sections.heading: What to check in an MYP tutor in Mumbai, beyond the subject
paragraphs: IB Gram verifies government photo identity, sights qualifications rather than accepting claims, holds a subject conversation with someone who knows the programme, and checks teaching history where it exists. For MYP there is an extra filter that matters more than any credential: whether the tutor has actually taught to criteria. Many excellent subject teachers in Mumbai have taught conventional syllabuses for twenty years and will quietly convert criterion work into chapter revision, because that is what they know.

Three questions expose this in under five minutes. Ask them to name the four criteria in the subject group your child is studying, which a tutor who has taught it will do without hesitating. Ask what they do with the task-specific clarification, and listen for whether they know what it is. Ask how they would raise a band in the communicating criterion without teaching any new content, which has a real answer and cannot be improvised. An IB MYP home tutor in Dahisar who answers all three is worth more than one with a longer list of degrees.

Because this age group is younger, two further checks are yours to make and they matter. Keep sessions in a shared room with the door open and an adult somewhere in the flat; a professional tutor will often suggest this before you do. And watch how the tutor speaks to your child in the first ten minutes, because at thirteen a student who feels talked down to will stop volunteering what she does not understand, and from that point the sessions are theatre.

Be wary of a tutor who offers a guaranteed grade, quotes a success rate, or implies he is the best IB tutor in Dahisar. We do not guarantee grades and publish no improvement statistics, which in the MYP is doubly true because bands are awarded by the student's own teachers against task-specific criteria. Anyone claiming to be able to move those reliably is describing influence they do not have. A tutor can improve the work; the school judges it.

sections.heading: From MYP Year 5 to the Diploma Programme: the transition Mumbai parents worry about most
paragraphs: The honest summary is that MYP prepares students well for two of the three things the Diploma Programme demands and barely at all for the third. It prepares them for independent investigation, because the inquiring-and-designing and investigating-patterns criteria have been asking for exactly that for five years. It prepares them for structured written reasoning, because the communicating criteria have been marking it. What it does not prepare them for is performing under timed examination conditions, because MYP students may sit very few of them.

That gap is specific and fixable, and it is worth starting in the final MYP year rather than the first DP year. A student who has never written for two hours against a clock does not know how long she takes, how her handwriting degrades, which questions she should skip, or what it feels like to run out of time. Four or five timed papers across the final MYP year, marked honestly, teaches all of that before it costs her anything. An IB MYP home tutor in Dahisar can run this alongside ordinary criterion work without disrupting it.

The second part of the transition is subject depth, and it is uneven. Mathematics and the sciences jump hardest, because the Diploma Programme assumes algebraic fluency and quantitative confidence that MYP assessment does not specifically reward. A student with strong bands in mathematics can still arrive in the Diploma Programme short of the manipulation speed the first term requires. The useful final-MYP-year work there is fluency practice: rearranging, indices, fractions and trigonometry done fast and accurately, which is dull and highly protective.

The personal project is the best rehearsal available for the Extended Essay (EE) and families underuse it. It teaches scoping a goal that can actually be achieved, keeping evidence of process as you go rather than reconstructing it, and writing honestly about what did not work. A student who learns those three things in the final MYP year arrives at the Extended Essay with the hardest habits already formed. A tutor's role is to ask the uncomfortable questions each week and to refuse, firmly, to help make the product.

sections.heading: What four weeks of MYP tuition in Mumbai should change
paragraphs: In four weeks, expect one criterion to move and the rest to stay where they are, and treat that as success. Criterion work is narrow by design: a student who could not structure an analysis can be taught to structure one in a month, and that shows up in the next marked task in that subject group. What should not happen is a general improvement claim with nothing specific attached. Ask an IB MYP home tutor in Dahisar at the start which criterion is the target and which marked task will show whether it worked.

Over a term, the thing to watch is transfer. A communicating criterion fixed in science should start showing up in individuals and societies, because the skill is the same wearing different clothes. If it does not transfer, the student has learned a format rather than a skill, and the tutor should be asked about it directly. Transfer is the honest test of whether MYP tuition is teaching or coaching, and it is visible on a report within two cycles.

Across a full MYP year, outcomes depend heavily on something no tutor controls: the student's own teachers award the bands against their own task-specific clarifications. We do not guarantee grades and will never publish an improvement rate, and in the middle years that reticence is not modesty. A tutor can improve the quality of the work a student submits. The judgement on that work belongs to the school, and a service claiming otherwise is claiming influence over someone else's marking.

The limits are worth stating plainly for this age group. A tutor cannot substitute for reading, and a Year 2 MYP student who reads nothing will not develop the analysis criterion whoever teaches her. A tutor cannot fix a language acquisition phase mismatch; that is a conversation with the coordinator. And an hour a week cannot compensate for a child who is exhausted by a long school day plus travel, which in this part of Mumbai is a real and common cause of weak bands that no tuition will touch.

sections.heading: Starting IB MYP home tuition in Dahisar: what the first session covers
paragraphs: Have four things ready: the most recent marked task with the criterion bands and the teacher's comments, the task-specific clarification that came with it, the current notebook or folder, and the school's unit plan for the term if you have it. The marked task with its clarification is the whole brief. A tutor holding both can see precisely where the student fell short of the band she was aiming for, which is a far better starting point than any conversation about how she finds the subject.

The first session should be spent reading and watching, not teaching. Expect the tutor to go through the folder, ask the student to explain what the task was asking in her own words, and then watch her attempt a short piece of similar work. Expect him to notice what she skips. Expect a plain statement at the end naming one criterion as the target and describing what the next four weeks will look like. One criterion, not four. A plan that promises to lift everything at once is not a plan.

What should not happen is a package of sessions to buy, a separately priced assessment, or any prediction about a final MYP result. Families arranging an IB private tutor Dahisar side for middle-years work should treat the first hour as their evaluation of the tutor, and should feel free to choose the second profile without giving a reason. If the tutor spoke for most of the hour, he has told you how he will run the rest of them.

From there the pattern is a fixed weekly slot early enough that the student is awake, work set and marked between sessions, the task-specific clarification read before each assignment, and a written review at two to four weeks naming whether the target criterion moved. There is no lock-in. If the review concludes the real issue is sleep, travel time or a phase placement rather than teaching, we will say so and point you at the coordinator instead.

faqs.question: What do IB tuition fees in Dahisar depend on for MYP work?
faqs.answer: MYP year, subject group and scarcity, and we will not publish a rate because the honest answer differs by case. Senior MYP years cost more than the early ones because the work is closer to Diploma Programme depth. Language acquisition at an unusual phase and design are the scarcest here, which raises them above mathematics or sciences. Personal project supervision in the final year is priced differently again, since it involves reading a journal between sessions rather than teaching an hour. Travel distance, slot timing and session length do the rest. Ask for the breakdown.

faqs.question: My son's report shows criterion letters and no percentage. How do I read it?
faqs.answer: Read each criterion separately and ignore any instinct to average them. Each one is a different skill: typically one covers knowledge, one covers investigating or analysing, one covers communicating, and one covers applying or reflecting. A strong band in the first with a weak band in the third means he knows the material and cannot present it, which needs writing structure rather than more content. The opposite profile needs the reverse. Then ask the teacher for the task-specific clarification from the task that produced the weak band, because it describes exactly what the top band required.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come home for a Year 2 MYP student straight after school?
faqs.answer: That is the slot to ask for, and it is the hardest to staff, so ask early. A twelve-year-old has a usable window in the late afternoon and very little left by half past seven, so matching a tutor who can arrive at five matters more than matching a marginally stronger tutor who can only come later. We shortlist from within Dahisar and Borivali for early slots because nobody is crossing the city at that hour reliably. Send the building name and visitor procedure so the first visit is not spent at the gate.

faqs.question: Does MYP tuition undermine the inquiry approach the school is using?
faqs.answer: It can, and that is a fair worry. Tuition undermines inquiry when a tutor gives answers, supplies a structure to copy, or works through a textbook chapter instead of the task the school set. It supports inquiry when the tutor asks the questions the student has not thought to ask, insists she explain her reasoning aloud, and makes her redraft rather than correcting for her. Ask any prospective tutor how he would handle a student who wants to be told the answer. The reply tells you which of those two you are hiring.

faqs.question: What exactly is the personal project, and can a tutor help with it?
faqs.answer: It is an independent piece of work in the final MYP year where the student sets a goal, keeps a process journal while pursuing it, produces something, and reports on the whole process against criteria. A tutor can help with scoping a goal that is actually achievable, with the discipline of journalling weekly rather than reconstructing it later, and with writing honestly about what went wrong. A tutor cannot choose the goal, make the product or write the report. The most common failure is an impressive product with a thin journal, and that is avoidable only early.

faqs.question: Will my daughter struggle moving from MYP Year 5 into the Diploma Programme?
faqs.answer: Probably in one specific area: timed examinations. MYP assessment is continuous and criterion-based, so a student may reach the Diploma Programme having rarely written for two hours against a clock. That is fixable with four or five honestly marked timed papers during the final MYP year. The second gap is quantitative fluency in mathematics and the sciences, where the Diploma assumes manipulation speed that MYP marking does not specifically reward. Investigation skills and written reasoning usually transfer well, which is the part MYP genuinely does better than most systems.

faqs.question: Can a tutor travel to Mira Road for a 5pm evening slot during the week?
faqs.answer: From within Mira Road or Dahisar, usually yes; from further south, a five o'clock arrival across the municipal boundary is difficult and we would rather not build a young student's slot around it. For Mira Road households we shortlist tutors already working that side, which keeps the arrival time honest. If the only strong profile for a scarce subject group lives further away, the realistic options are a weekend morning session or short online check-ins, and we will put both in front of you rather than promise an evening that will slip by October.

faqs.question: Is one tutor enough for several MYP subject groups at once?
faqs.answer: Sometimes in the early MYP years, rarely in the senior ones. In Years 1 and 2 a strong generalist who understands criteria can genuinely support mathematics, sciences and humanities together, and that is often the sensible arrangement. By Years 4 and 5 the subject depth has diverged enough that a generalist starts guessing, particularly in sciences and mathematics. If the weakness is a single criterion appearing across several subject groups, one tutor is right regardless of year, because you are buying a skill rather than three syllabuses.

faqs.question: She has never sat a timed exam. Should we be worried?
faqs.answer: Worried is too strong; prepared is better. The risk is not that she cannot perform under time, it is that she has no information about herself under time: how long she takes, which questions to leave, how her handwriting holds up, what running out feels like. All of that is learnable in four or five sessions spread across the final MYP year, and it is far cheaper to learn it there than in the first Diploma Programme mock. Ask a tutor to mark those papers honestly rather than generously, because a flattering mark teaches nothing.

faqs.question: Do you cover Borivali East and Borivali West for MYP as well as Dahisar?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for MYP the three work almost as one. Borivali East and Dahisar share the same tutor pool entirely, which matters most for the early-evening slots younger students need. Borivali West adds the station-side tutors and is comfortable in both directions. Because so many requests here are for a criterion rather than a syllabus, the match is often less about geography than about which tutor has actually taught that subject group at that MYP year, and we will tell you if that means looking at a weekend slot instead.

faqs.question: What should four weeks of MYP tuition actually produce?
faqs.answer: One named criterion moving on one marked task, plus a written note explaining why. Agree the target criterion and the task that will test it before the first session, so that the review at four weeks has something to measure. Alongside that you should see her able to say what a task is asking in her own words, and bringing the task-specific clarification to sessions without being reminded. A month that produces a general sense of progress with no criterion named and no task identified has produced nothing you can act on.

faqs.question: What happens if the MYP tutor is not the right fit?
faqs.answer: Tell us and we change the match, with no switching fee and no need to make the case twice. In the middle years the most common reason is tone rather than knowledge: a thirteen-year-old who feels patronised stops admitting what she does not understand, and from there the hour is wasted however good the teaching is. Be specific when you tell us, because "she has gone quiet" leads to a different replacement than "he never looks at her folder". Nobody treats a change as a complaint, and most matches that change work second time.

sections.heading: How an IB MYP home tutor in Fort is matched to one criterion
paragraphs: The first thing we do with a Middle Years Programme (MYP) enquiry is ask for the report and then read it properly, which parents are often surprised by. An MYP subject report gives separate marks against four criteria, and those four assess genuinely different things. In the Sciences a student can be strong on knowing and understanding while losing most of her available credit on processing and evaluating data, which is a write-up problem rather than a science problem. In Mathematics she can be solid on knowing and understanding and weak on investigating patterns, which means she can execute and cannot generalise. Those two students need completely different tutors.

The sequence runs like this. 1. We establish the MYP year, Years 1 to 5, and the subject group, because a Year 2 enquiry and a Year 5 enquiry are different pieces of work. 2. We read the report criterion by criterion and identify the single lowest strand rather than the overall picture. 3. We ask for one marked assessed task with the teacher's criterion comments still on it, since the comment explains the mark in a way the number cannot. 4. We shortlist tutors who have taught that subject group in the MYP specifically, and who already work inside South Mumbai. 5. The first session diagnoses against that criterion and ends with a written finding in plain language.

Step two is the one that saves families the most money. A parent reading a row of marks concludes that her son is weak in Individuals and Societies and asks for a history tutor. Read criterion by criterion, the pattern is frequently that he knows the content perfectly and loses credit on the criterion that asks him to organise and communicate an argument in writing, which is the same weakness showing up in Language and Literature and in Sciences on his report as well. That is one problem across three subjects, not three problems, and it is fixed by one tutor working on written structure rather than by three subject specialists.

What you get back is a short written note in English rather than in MYP vocabulary: which criterion is losing credit, whether the same weakness appears in other subjects, what the next four sessions will do, and what we think is not a tutoring problem at all. Parents searching IB tutors near me Fort for MYP help are usually looking for subject content. The useful intervention at this stage is almost always narrower and cheaper than the one they came for.

sections.heading: What are the eight MYP subject groups, and which matters here?
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme runs across five years, covering roughly the middle grades, and organises learning into eight subject groups: Language and Literature, Language Acquisition, Individuals and Societies, Sciences, Mathematics, Arts, Physical and Health Education, and Design. Each is assessed against four criteria, each criterion has its own published descriptors, and the names of the criteria differ between subject groups, which is the first thing that confuses parents.

Most of the tutoring demand in Fort concentrates in four of the eight: Mathematics, Sciences, Language and Literature, and Individuals and Societies. That is not because the others matter less but because they are where parents can see trouble on a report and feel able to act. Design is the group families most often overlook, and it is worth knowing that it carries a genuine assessed process with its own criteria rather than being an optional extra. A student losing credit in Design is usually losing it on the criterion covering the development of ideas, not on the finished artefact.

The structural feature that distinguishes the MYP from what comes before and after is that it is organised around concepts and inquiry rather than around content coverage. Units are built on a statement of inquiry and a global context, and students are assessed on approaches to learning skills alongside subject knowledge. Interdisciplinary units ask them to connect two subject groups. All of that is pedagogically coherent and it has one practical consequence for a parent: there is no fixed syllabus list you can tick off, which makes it much harder to tell whether your child is behind.

Some schools enter MYP Year 5 students for the programme's own on-screen assessments and ePortfolios, and many do not, so ask your school directly rather than assuming either way. What your child's school assesses, how it reports, and which criteria it uses in each subject should all come from the school's own criteria sheets and its coordinator. This page is about the MYP specifically; the Diploma Programme and its Higher Level, Standard Level, Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge requirements belong to sibling pages, and so do the IGCSE years, which are a different system entirely.

sections.heading: How do you read an MYP report that is not a percentage?
paragraphs: Read it one criterion at a time and ignore the overall figure, because the overall figure is a summary of four separate judgements and tells you nothing about which one to act on. A mark against a criterion is a judgement about the quality of a specific capability, measured against published descriptors, and it does not convert into a percentage however much a parent would like it to. The useful question is never how well is she doing but which criterion is lowest, and is the same criterion low in more than one subject.

The criteria divide broadly into knowing, inquiring, communicating and reflecting, though the exact names change by subject group. In Mathematics, knowing and understanding covers whether she can execute, while investigating patterns asks whether she can find and justify a generalisation, communicating asks whether her reasoning is legible to a reader, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts asks whether she can model a situation. In the Sciences the four cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing an investigation, processing and evaluating data, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In Language and Literature they cover analysing, organising, producing text and using language.

The single most common MYP weakness we see in Fort families is the communicating or organising criterion, across every subject group at once. The student understands the material, answers questions correctly in conversation, and produces written work that is disorganised, under-explained or missing the reasoning that earns the credit. This is why a parent's instinct to hire three subject tutors is usually wrong: one tutor working on written structure, paragraph purpose and the discipline of explaining reasoning will lift three subjects simultaneously, and it is the cheapest intervention available in the whole programme.

The second most common is the inquiring and designing or investigating criterion, which asks a student to pose a question, plan how to answer it and justify her choices. This is a skill almost nothing in a child's earlier schooling has required of her, and it is the direct precursor of everything that matters in the Diploma Programme: the scientific investigation, the mathematical exploration, the Extended Essay. An MYP subject groups tutor in Fort who works on this criterion in Year 3 is doing more for a student's Diploma Programme outcome than any amount of content coaching in Year 5.
